subtopics.title: The US-Saudi 123 Agreement
subtopics.summary: The US and Saudi Arabia signed a Section 123 Civil Nuclear Cooperation Agreement with a bilateral safeguards arrangement, for 30 years. Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954 makes such agreements a legally binding prerequisite for significant US nuclear cooperation. The deal is reportedly linked to Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords and normalising relations with Israel.
facts: Signed for 30 years by US Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.
Named after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, 1954.
A 123 Agreement is a legally binding prerequisite for significant US nuclear cooperation with another country.
Cooperation may cover reactors, nuclear materials, components, equipment, technology and technical expertise.
Bilateral Safeguards Arrangement ensures civilian nuclear materials are not diverted towards weapons.
Saudi Arabia may undertake uranium enrichment in facilities developed with US support, subject to safeguards.
The agreement does not require Saudi Arabia to adopt the IAEA Additional Protocol.
The agreement is subject to a review period of 90 legislative days by the US Congress.
The deal is reportedly linked to Riyadh joining the Abraham Accords and normalising relations with Israel.

subtopics.title: Saudi Arabia's Nuclear Vision
subtopics.summary: Saudi Arabia's nuclear programme is built on four drivers: energy diversification, large-scale desalination, meeting cooling demand and strategic technology development. The Kingdom signed the NPT in 1988 and launched its National Atomic Energy Project in 2017. The new deal drops the earlier Israel normalisation condition and allows flexibility on domestic enrichment.
facts: Nuclear power lets Saudi Arabia reduce its heavy dependence on crude oil and natural gas for electricity.
The nuclear programme provides the massive energy input needed for large-scale water desalination.
Nuclear-generated electricity provides a steady supply for air-conditioning and cooling systems.
A nuclear programme grants access to advanced technology and reinforces Saudi status as a regional energy power.
Saudi Arabia signed the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty in 1988.
Saudi Arabia launched its National Atomic Energy Project in 2017.
The earlier Gold Standard required no domestic uranium enrichment or reprocessing, and normalised ties with Israel.
The new deal drops the Israel normalisation condition and allows flexibility for US-supported domestic enrichment.

subtopics.title: Nuclear Weapons History and Treaties
subtopics.summary: Nuclear weapons were developed in the US-led Manhattan Project, with the Trinity test in July 1945 and bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. Treaties then tried to limit testing and spread, including the PTBT (1963), NPT (1968), CTBT (1996) and TPNW (2017). The IAEA (1957) and the NSG (1974-75) were created to manage peaceful use and export controls.
facts: The Manhattan Project was a secret US-led programme with the UK and Canada; Gen. Leslie Groves led engineering and J. Robert Oppenheimer led science.
The Trinity Test in July 1945 was the first-ever nuclear explosion, conducted in the New Mexico desert.
Little Boy (uranium gun-type) was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945; Fat Man (plutonium implosion-type) was dropped on Nagasaki on 9 August 1945.
The Partial Test Ban Treaty (1963) banned tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater, but not underground.
The Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (1968) was signed to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.
The IAEA, established in 1957, promotes peaceful uses of atomic energy and oversees safeguards.
The Nuclear Suppliers Group (1974-75) was formed to control the export of nuclear materials and technology.
The CTBT (1996) was adopted by the UN to ban all nuclear explosions and has not yet entered into force.
The TPNW (2017) entered into force in 2021 and is the first legally binding treaty to comprehensively ban nuclear weapons; nuclear powers have not joined.
North Korea withdrew from the NPT in 2003 and later conducted nuclear tests.

subtopics.title: India's Atomic Energy Journey
subtopics.summary: India's programme was organised through the Atomic Energy Commission (1948) and the Department of Atomic Energy (1954), with Dr Homi J. Bhabha leading the AEC. Key milestones include the 1974 Pokhran-I test and the 1998 Pokhran-II tests. The 2008 Indo-US 123 Agreement ended India's nuclear isolation and was a landmark precedent.
facts: The Atomic Energy Commission was set up in 1948, with Dr Homi J. Bhabha as its chairman.
The Department of Atomic Energy was created in 1954 under the Prime Minister's Office.
The Atomic Energy Act, 1962 is India's primary law for nuclear energy.
Tarapur Atomic Power Station, India's first commercial nuclear plant, was commissioned in 1969 under Atoms for Peace.
Pokhran-I (1974), the Smiling Buddha test, was India's first peaceful nuclear explosion.
Dhruva, India's largest research reactor, was commissioned at BARC in 1985.
Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti) in 1998 led to India being declared a nuclear-weapon state.
India's Nuclear Doctrine, adopted in 2003, follows No First Use and Credible Minimum Deterrence.
The Indo-US Civil Nuclear Agreement (123 Agreement), signed in 2008, ended India's nuclear isolation.
India is a Non-NPT nuclear weapons state, which makes the 2008 agreement a landmark precedent.

subtopics.title: PM's State Visit and Key Outcomes
subtopics.summary: The Prime Minister of India concluded a State Visit to Indonesia, reinforcing the India-Indonesia Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The visit brought the Prime Minister an Indonesian honour and several agreements covering defence, industry, health, disaster management and agriculture.
facts: Bintang Republik Indonesia Adipurna is Indonesia's highest civilian honour.
The Prime Minister was conferred the 35th Bintang Republik Indonesia Adipurna.
The Prime Minister is only the 2nd Indian PM to receive it, after Jawaharlal Nehru.
Indonesia signed a contract worth around USD 200 million for 2 batteries of BrahMos.
Indonesia placed its 1st international order for the indigenous Astra Beyond missile.
SAIL agreed to establish a Stainless Steel Slab Manufacturing Facility in Indonesia.
CDSCO and its Indonesian counterpart agreed to strengthen medical product regulation.
NDMA signed an MoU with Indonesia's Disaster Management Agency on preparedness and response.
India announced supply of 100 tonnes of high-quality wheat seeds (DWR-162).

subtopics.title: Strategic Partnership: Defence, Maritime and Digital
subtopics.summary: Indonesia occupies a pivotal position in India's Act East Policy, SAGAR vision and Indo-Pacific Strategy, close to the Strait of Malacca. Cooperation covers joint military exercises, maritime awareness, satellite support and digital commerce.
facts: Indonesia is India's 2nd largest trading partner within ASEAN.
Indonesia is the largest economy in ASEAN.
Major military exercises include IND-INDO CORPAT, Garuda Shakti, Samudra Shakti, Milan and Komodo.
A 3rd India-Indonesia Security Dialogue has been proposed to strengthen defence consultations.
India and Indonesia agreed to jointly develop Sabang Port, near the entrance to the Strait of Malacca.
Malacca is one of the world's busiest maritime chokepoints.
Indonesia will post a Liaison Officer at IFC-IOR to improve Maritime Domain Awareness.
ISRO and Indonesia's BRIN jointly operate the Biak Telemetry, Tracking and Command Facility.
Indonesia Open Network was inspired by India's Open Network for Digital Commerce model.

subtopics.title: Prambanan Temple and Shared Heritage
subtopics.summary: The Prambanan Temple Complex in Yogyakarta, locally known as Roro Jonggrang, is Indonesia's largest Hindu temple complex and India is supporting its conservation. Shared heritage and cultural diplomacy are reflected in the Tagore-Dewantara Year and a planned IIM Bangalore branch campus.
facts: Prambanan is locally known as Roro Jonggrang.
Prambanan is the largest Hindu temple complex in Indonesia.
Prambanan is the 2nd largest in Southeast Asia, after Angkor Wat in Cambodia.
It was built in the 9th and 10th centuries CE under the Sanjaya Dynasty (Mataram Kingdom).
It is dedicated to the Hindu Trinity of Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma.
British surveyor Colin Mackenzie formally rediscovered the ruins in 1811.
India will provide technical support for conservation of the Prambanan Temple Complex.
2026-27 is declared the Tagore-Dewantara Year of India-Indonesia Cultural and Educational Diplomacy.
The Tagore-Dewantara Year commemorates the centenary of Rabindranath Tagore's visit to Indonesia.
Approval was announced for an IIM Bangalore branch campus at Singhasari Special Economic Zone, East Java.
India presented a replica of the Nalanda Copper Plate to strengthen shared civilisational links.

subtopics.title: Non-Aligned Movement (NAM)
subtopics.summary: NAM is a group of states not formally aligned with or against any major power bloc, founded in 1961 in Belgrade, Serbia. It is rooted in the Ten Principles of the 1955 Bandung Conference, and India and Indonesia were both founding members.
facts: NAM is a group of states not formally aligned with or against any major power bloc.
NAM was founded in 1961 in Belgrade, Serbia.
NAM is based on the Ten Principles of the Bandung Conference, 1955.
Founding fathers include Jawaharlal Nehru (India), Sukarno (Indonesia), Josip Broz Tito (Yugoslavia) and Kwame Nkrumah (Ghana).
NAM emphasised the 4Ds: Detente, Disarmament, Decolonisation and Development of the Third World.
NAM contributed to the 1963 Partial Test Ban Treaty through declarations on nuclear testing and non-proliferation.
NAM helped create several nuclear-weapon-free zones.
NAM advocated for the Global South and supported anti-apartheid in South Africa and Namibia.
NAM has supported India's candidature at the UNSC.
NAM failed to halt the arms race and to resolve regional conflicts such as Iran-Pakistan and Russia-Ukraine.

subtopics.title: Three Bills and Their Scope
subtopics.summary: The 130th Constitution Amendment Bill, 2025 is one of three Bills tabled by the Home Minister, and together the Bills propose the removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers under certain conditions. A Joint Parliamentary Committee is examining the Bill and is expected to finalise and adopt its report. The other two Bills are the Government of Union Territories (Amendment) Bill, 2025 and the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2025.
facts: Introduced in 2025 as the 130th Constitution Amendment Bill
Three Bills tabled by the Home Minister
Bill 1: Constitution (One Hundred and Thirtieth Amendment) Bill, 2025
Bill 2: Government of Union Territories (Amendment) Bill, 2025
Bill 3: Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2025
The Bills propose removal of Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers under certain conditions
Joint Parliamentary Committee (JPC) is examining the 130th Amendment Bill
The JPC is expected to finalise and adopt its report

subtopics.title: Removal Conditions and Authorities
subtopics.summary: The Bill's trigger is arrest and detention for 30 consecutive days on an offence punishable with five years or more. The removal authority depends on the office: the President for Union Ministers, the Governor for State Ministers and Chief Ministers, and the Lieutenant Governor for Delhi and Jammu & Kashmir. If no advice is given for a Union Minister, the Minister automatically ceases to hold office on the 31st day.
facts: Trigger: arrested and detained for 30 consecutive days
The offence must be punishable with imprisonment of five years or more
Union Ministers: Article 75 is amended
Union Ministers: the President removes on the advice of the Prime Minister
If no advice is given, the Minister automatically ceases to hold office on the 31st day
A removed Minister can be reappointed after release from custody
State Ministers and Chief Ministers: Article 164, removal authority is the Governor
Delhi Ministers: Article 239AA, removal authority is the Lieutenant Governor
Union Territory Ministers: Government of Union Territories Act, 1963, removal authority is the Administrator or Lieutenant Governor
Jammu & Kashmir Ministers: J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019, removal authority is the Lieutenant Governor

subtopics.title: Governance Implications and Concerns
subtopics.summary: The Bill is presented as strengthening ethical governance by stopping leaders from holding power while facing serious criminal charges. It is also described as bridging a gap in the Representation of the People Act, which disqualifies legislators only after conviction. The booklet records several concerns, including misuse of arrests against opposition-led states, a threat to federalism and the presumption of innocence.
facts: The Bill upholds constitutional morality and ethical governance
It stops leaders from retaining power while facing serious criminal charges
It removes the 'governance from jail' anomaly
It protects public trust by acting against criminalisation of politics
It bridges a legal gap: the RPA disqualifies only post-conviction, while the Bill addresses interim arrests
Concern: the Centre could destabilise opposition-led states through targeted arrests
Concern: the Bill reduces the autonomy of elected state leaders, threatening federalism
Concern: removal based solely on detention contravenes 'innocent until proven guilty'
Concern: ED and CBI could be exploited to arrest leaders on weak charges

subtopics.title: Representation of People Act and Court Rulings
subtopics.summary: Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 sets different disqualification rules for convictions, depending on the offence and the sentence. Section 8(4), which protected sitting members who appeal within three months, was struck down by the Supreme Court. Supreme Court rulings on ministers with criminal backgrounds and on who can add grounds of disqualification form the wider legal background.
facts: Section 8(1): conviction for promoting enmity, rape, terrorist acts or insulting the national flag means six years' disqualification on mere conviction
Section 8(2): conviction for hoarding or dowry offences with a sentence of at least six months; the bar continues six years after release
Section 8(3): conviction for other offences with a sentence of not less than two years; disqualification till six years after release
Section 8(4): sitting MPs and MLAs can continue if they appeal within three months, until the term ends or the appeal is decided, whichever is earlier
Lily Thomas v. Union of India: the Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4) as invalid
Manoj Narula v. Union of India (2014): no constitutional bar exists on appointing ministers with a criminal background
Public Interest Foundation PIL (2018): only Parliament can legislate on disqualification; courts cannot add new grounds
V Senthil Balaji case (2025): a Tamil Nadu minister reappointed post-bail had to choose between freedom and office, and he stepped down while bail continued
Law Commission 170th Report: recommended disqualification at the framing of charges for offences punishable with five years or more

subtopics.title: Passage of a Constitution Amendment Bill
subtopics.summary: A Constitution amendment Bill can be introduced in either House, but it must be passed by both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha. Once passed, it is presented to the President, who is bound to give consent, and the Bill then becomes an Act. The booklet also links the process to the Anti-Defection Law and related constitutional articles.
facts: The Bill can be introduced either in Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
The Bill must be passed by both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Lok Sabha strength is 545 members
In a tie, the Presiding Officer of a house can cast his or her vote
The passed Bill is presented to the President
The President is bound to give consent
After assent the Bill becomes an Act
Related provisions: Articles 102 and 191, the Anti-Defection Law and the Lily Thomas case

topics.title: Autonomous Hill Development Councils expanded across Ladakh

subtopics.title: Why the AHDC expansion matters
subtopics.summary: The Ladakh Administration has approved Autonomous Hill Development Councils (AHDCs) in all 7 districts after an in-principle agreement with the Ministry of Home Affairs. The move follows Ladakh becoming a Union Territory without a Legislative Assembly in 2019, which makes decentralised local institutions central to governance. Before the expansion, elected councils existed only in Leh and Kargil.
facts: Ladakh Administration approved AHDCs in all 7 districts
In-principle agreement with the Ministry of Home Affairs
Agreement aims to extend Article 371 constitutional safeguards to the UT

subtopics.title: Legal basis, powers and finances of AHDCs
subtopics.summary: AHDCs function under the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Act and are created through legislation, applying only in Ladakh. Section 3(1) empowers the Government to establish a Council in every district through an official notification. Their powers are mainly administrative and developmental, covering land allotment, district cadre recruitment and promotions, and district development planning. Each AHDC maintains a Council Fund and can levy taxes, fees and other lawful charges for local governance.
facts: Functions under the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Act
Created through legislation and applicable only in Ladakh
Section 3(1): Government can set up a Council in every district by official notification
Power over land allotment
Power over district cadre recruitment and promotions
Power over district development planning
Sectors include health, education, tourism, infrastructure and social welfare
Each AHDC maintains a Council Fund
Can levy taxes, fees and other lawful charges for local governance
No judicial authority

subtopics.title: AHDCs versus 6th Schedule councils and Article 371
subtopics.summary: AHDCs and 6th Schedule Autonomous District Councils are both local bodies, but they differ in how they are created, where they apply and what powers they hold. AHDCs are created through legislation and apply only in Ladakh, while 6th Schedule councils have constitutional status under Articles 244(2) and 275(1). Article 371 and Articles 371A to 371J, under Part XXI, provide special safeguards for indigenous culture, customary laws, land rights and local employment.

6th Schedule councils: constitutional status under Articles 244(2) and 275(1)
6th Schedule councils apply in notified tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura
AHDCs: mainly administrative and developmental powers, no judicial authority

subtopics.title: Ladakh's profile, demands and 2025 reservation rules
subtopics.summary: Ladakh, known as the Land of High Passes or Maryul, has been administered by the Government of India as a Union Territory since 31 October 2019. Its people demand inclusion under the 6th Schedule, restrictions on land ownership to prevent outsider influx, and a Legislative Assembly. A reservation regulation approved on 2 June 2025 and effective from 3 June 2025 raises the total reservation cap to 85 per cent, with EWS quotas excluded.

Administered by the Government of India as a UT since 31 October 2019
Capital: Leh, with Kargil as the winter capital
Demand: inclusion under the 6th Schedule for constitutional protection

subtopics.title: Policy Overview and Targets
subtopics.summary: Delhi EV Policy 2.0 was notified by the Government of NCT of Delhi and is scheduled to come into force from 1 July 2026, remaining effective until 31 March 2030. It builds upon the achievements of Delhi EV Policy 2020 and aims to turn Delhi into a leading electric mobility hub. The policy targets at least 30% electrification of Delhi's total vehicle fleet by 31 March 2030, with a focus on high-usage and high-emission transport segments.

In force from 1 July 2026
Effective until 31 March 2030
Builds upon the achievements of Delhi EV Policy 2020
Electrification target: at least 30% of Delhi's total vehicle fleet by 31 March 2030

Objective: widespread adoption of zero-emission vehicles
Objective: reduce urban air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions

subtopics.title: Registration Rules and Phase-out
subtopics.summary: New registrations in Delhi move to electric models in stages. From 1 January 2027 only electric 3-wheelers and electric N1 category light commercial trucks can be newly registered, and from 1 April 2028 new 2-wheeler registrations are restricted to electric models. Existing petrol and diesel vehicles may keep operating until the end of their prescribed service life. Schools must also electrify part of their bus fleets.

From 1 April 2028: registration of new 2-wheelers restricted exclusively to electric models

Schools must convert at least 10% of their bus fleet into electric buses within 2 years of policy implementation
Long-term objective: 30% electrification of school bus fleets by 2030

subtopics.title: Investment, Support and Charging
subtopics.summary: The policy plans total investment of approximately 15,000 crore. Government support is restricted exclusively to battery electric vehicles and not to hybrid vehicles. The plan includes installing over 30,000 public charging stations across Delhi. Financial support and investment is handled by the Delhi Transport Department, and infrastructure development by Delhi Transco Limited.

subtopics.title: National Schemes: NEMMP, FAME and PM E-DRIVE
subtopics.summary: Delhi's policy sits within national electric mobility efforts. The National Electric Mobility Mission Plan was launched in 2013, and the government committed to achieve 30% e-mobility by 2030. FAME India, launched by the Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises, is part of that mission plan and offers subsidies for several vehicle types. PM E-DRIVE, launched in 2024 with the Ministry of Heavy Industries as nodal ministry, builds on FAME-II and the Electric Mobility Promotion Scheme 2024.

topics.title: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana

subtopics.title: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana scheme
subtopics.summary: PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana is a rooftop solar scheme launched in 2024 and described as the world's largest domestic rooftop solar initiative. Its aim is to provide free electricity up to 300 units to households by installing rooftop solar panels. The scheme offers a subsidy of up to 40% on panel installation and targets 1 crore households by 2027, with the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy as nodal ministry. A parallel Model Solar Village initiative asks each district to establish one such village to promote energy self-reliance.

subtopics.title: International Solar Alliance (ISA)
subtopics.summary: The International Solar Alliance (ISA) is a treaty-based intergovernmental organisation of solar-rich countries lying between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn. It was launched jointly by India and France in 2015 during COP21 in Paris. Its membership comprises 112 members and 15 signatory countries, and its headquarters is in Gurugram.

India overtook Japan to become the world's third largest solar power producer in 2025. The country also hosts Bhadla Solar Park, India's largest solar plant at 2245 MW, and Omkareshwar, India's largest floating solar plant at 600 MW.

subtopics.title: Global initiatives and climate commitments

topics.title: Proposed NFSA Amendment for AAY Households

subtopics.title: Proposed AAY Entitlement Change
subtopics.summary: The Union Government has proposed amending Section 3(1) of the National Food Security Act 2013 to change foodgrain entitlement for Antyodaya Anna Yojana households. The current rule gives each AAY household a fixed 35 kg per month irrespective of family size. The proposal shifts the basis to individuals, at 7 kg per person per month, with a maximum of 35 kg per household.

subtopics.title: Rationale and Limits of the Amendment
subtopics.summary: The Union Government argues that the household-based AAY entitlement creates inequities within the category. Small households receive more foodgrain per person than larger ones, and the amendment would make distribution proportional to household size. The government also says the change reduces disparities with Priority Household beneficiaries, but the amendment does not address inclusion errors.

topics.title: India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA)

subtopics.title: Scope and Entry into Force
subtopics.summary: The India-UK CETA came into force on 15 July 2026, together with the Double Contribution Convention. The booklet calls it a next-generation free trade agreement that goes beyond conventional tariff reduction to cover market access, regulatory transparency and economic partnership. Its coverage spans goods and services, digital trade, investment, government procurement, labour, environment, innovation, SMEs and regulatory cooperation. It is also the first Indian FTA to give tariff concessions on imported passenger vehicles through tariff rate quotas.

subtopics.title: Tariff Cuts and Market Access
subtopics.summary: India plans to cut duties on 90% of tariff lines, with 85% becoming tariff-free within 10 years. Indian exports get zero-duty access for 99% of products, while auto import tariffs fall to 10% under a quota system from over 100%. Whisky and gin tariffs drop from 150% to 75% and reduce to 40% by the 10th year. The deal also adds 100 annual visas for Indian professionals, and bilateral trade of USD 56.8 billion is expected to double by 2030.

subtopics.title: Double Contribution Convention
subtopics.summary: The Double Contribution Convention came into force along with CETA and is aimed at social security contributions. Eligible Indian professionals and employers are exempt from UK National Insurance contributions for up to 5 years. The exemption applies provided contributions continue in India. The purpose is to ensure professionals avoid paying social security contributions in both India and the UK.

subtopics.title: Brexit and Trade Realignment
subtopics.summary: The India-UK FTA is part of Britain's post-Brexit strategy. The UK joined the EU in 1973 and formally left it on 31 January 2020, losing EU market access in the process. The UK and other western nations are diversifying trade away from China, with India as a China-plus-one alternative. India also moved away from RCEP towards bilateral FTAs such as the UK deal.

subtopics.title: Polymer Banknotes: Concept and Proposal
subtopics.summary: Polymer banknotes are printed on a specialised plastic substrate, primarily BOPP, instead of cotton-based banknote paper. RBI has revived a proposal for such notes that was first made in 2009, and BRBNMPL invited global bids for the polymer substrate. Australia was the first country to introduce a complete series of polymer banknotes, in 1988.

subtopics.title: Advantages of Polymer Notes
subtopics.summary: Polymer notes are more resistant to tearing, less vulnerable to water and moisture, and more durable under frequent circulation. They can carry advanced anti-counterfeiting features that are much harder to replicate than on paper. Because individual notes last longer, fewer new notes need to be manufactured to keep supply steady.
facts: More resistant to tearing.
Less vulnerable to water and moisture.
More durable under frequent circulation.
Capable of incorporating advanced anti-counterfeiting features.
Polymer notes remain usable for significantly longer periods.
Longer life means less frequent replacement cycles.
Fewer new notes need to be manufactured and issued to keep supply steady.
Polymer substrates allow security features that are much harder to replicate than on paper.
Less frequent replacement lowers the long-term environmental footprint.

subtopics.title: Costs, Supply Chain and Environmental Challenges
subtopics.summary: Polymer notes cost significantly more to produce than paper currency, and their production cost is tied to global oil prices. The notes are made from polypropylene, and reliance on imported polypropylene creates import dependency. Plastic waste needs a specialised collection and recycling system, and the transition requires changes to ATMs, vending machines and cash-handling machines.

Production cost is tied to global oil prices.
Polymer notes are made from polypropylene.
Reliance on imported polypropylene creates import dependency.
Unlike cotton-based paper, polymer notes raise concerns about plastic waste.
Plastic waste needs an effective specialised collection and recycling system.
Transition requires recalibration of ATMs, currency vending machines and automated cash-handling machines.
Changing to polymer notes creates substantial secondary expenses for banking and retail infrastructure.

subtopics.title: Currency Management and Printing in India
subtopics.summary: Currency and coinage fall under the Union List, and the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 provides the principal legal framework for issuing banknotes. RBI issues notes, estimates currency requirements and ensures circulation of good-quality notes. SPMCIL and BRBNMPL together operate four presses that print all banknotes in India.

RBI introduced the Clean Note Policy in 1999.
Government designs and mints coins, and RBI distributes them through its currency management network.

subtopics.title: Summit Outcomes
subtopics.summary: The 16th India-Japan Annual Summit was held in New Delhi during the first official India visit of Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, from July 1 to 3, 2026. The summit produced outcomes in defence, economic security, energy, artificial intelligence, trade and disaster risk reduction. Some outcomes launch new programmes, while others are agreements to convene further meetings or to review existing arrangements.

subtopics.summary: The Mumbai-Ahmedabad High-Speed Rail is a flagship India-Japan project that uses Shinkansen technology and forms part of India's National Rail Plan 2030. subtopics.title: Green Hydrogen and the National Green Hydrogen Mission
subtopics.summary: Hydrogen is the most common element in nature but exists only in combination with other elements, so it must be extracted from compounds such as water. Green hydrogen is made by splitting water through electrolysis using an electrolyser powered by renewable energy, and the booklet says it is not commercially viable at present. The National Green Hydrogen Mission, with the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy as nodal ministry, aims to decarbonise sectors and build domestic manufacturing.

subtopics.title: Evolution of the SDGs
subtopics.summary: The idea of sustainable development was defined in 1987 and then built into successive global commitments. Milestones such as the Millennium Development Goals, the Johannesburg Summit and Rio+20 moved the agenda forward. The 2015 adoption of the 2030 Agenda introduced 17 SDGs supported by 169 targets.

subtopics.title: Earth Summit 1992 and its outcomes
subtopics.summary: The UN Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro, popularly called the Earth Summit, aimed to integrate environmental protection with sustainable development. Its key outcomes were the Rio Declaration, Agenda 21 and the Forest Principles. The Rio Declaration sets out guiding principles, Agenda 21 is a non-binding action plan, and the Forest Principles are non-legally binding.

subtopics.title: Climate finance
subtopics.summary: Climate finance refers to financing from public, private or alternative sources that supports mitigation and adaptation against climate change. It rests on the Polluter Pays principle and CBDR-RC, and multilateral climate funds are coordinated by the UNFCCC. Persistent challenges include gaps between national needs and funding, slow approvals and much lower per-capita approved funding for Least Developed Countries.

subtopics.title: Mission and Orbit Basics
subtopics.summary: Skyroot Aerospace of Hyderabad launched Vikram-1 on Mission Aagaman, its maiden flight, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota. The booklet also separates sub-orbital rockets, which do not place a satellite into orbit, from orbital rockets, which do.

subtopics.summary: Vikram-1 carries scientific, technological, commercial and symbolic payloads. quizzes.title: The 123 deal: MCQ check
quizzes.passage: Saudi Arabia and the United States have signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement commonly called the 123 Agreement. The name comes from a section of a US law, the Atomic Energy Act of 1954. Under such an agreement, the United States can transfer nuclear reactors, nuclear materials, components, equipment, technology and technical expertise to a partner country. Because this framework is a legal precondition for significant nuclear cooperation, the deal therefore has significance beyond ordinary trade. Reports also link it to a regional political question, namely whether Riyadh will move toward ties with Israel. Saudi Arabia is a long-standing party to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty and has pursued a national atomic energy programme. Nuclear power is part of the Kingdom's wider energy planning. The new arrangement includes a bilateral safeguards system meant to ensure that civilian materials are not diverted to weapons. It also opens a possibility that Saudi Arabia could enrich uranium in facilities developed with US support, subject to agreed verification. The agreement is subject to a review period by the US Congress. Earlier, Washington had set a stricter standard for such cooperation, and the new deal relaxes parts of it. India's 2008 agreement with the United States is often cited as an earlier precedent in this field.

quizzes.title: Nuclear treaties and tests: TITA check
quizzes.passage: The nuclear age began during the Second World War, when a secret research effort led by the United States produced the first atomic bombs. The United Kingdom and Canada also took part in that effort. The first explosion took place in the New Mexico desert, and bombs were then dropped on two Japanese cities, after which Japan surrendered. Nuclear research in these years was kept highly secret. Other nuclear powers soon followed, and one later explosion set a record for size that still stands. Governments then responded with a set of agreements. One early treaty banned tests in the atmosphere, outer space and underwater, but not underground. Another treaty aimed to stop the spread of weapons, while a later UN treaty sought to ban all nuclear explosions, though it has not entered into force. In the late twentieth century, several countries outside the main treaties conducted tests. North Korea withdrew from one treaty and carried out its own tests. A treaty banning nuclear weapons completely became legally binding after a few years, though major nuclear powers have not joined it. A UN agency was also created to promote peaceful uses of atomic energy and to oversee safeguards. Today these agreements shape debates over which countries may acquire nuclear technology.

quizzes.title: Removal Conditions Check
quizzes.passage: The 130th Constitution Amendment Bill, 2025, is one of three Bills tabled by the Home Minister, and a Joint Parliamentary Committee is currently examining it. The Bill responds to a situation in which a political office-holder continues in office while facing serious criminal charges. It proposes that a minister who is held in custody on such charges can be removed from office. The proposal reaches several categories of leaders. These include Union Ministers, State Ministers and Chief Ministers, and also the Chief Minister and Ministers of Delhi, Ministers of Union Territories and Ministers of Jammu & Kashmir. Each category is governed by its own legal basis, so the same principle is applied through different constitutional and statutory provisions. The Bill specifies who holds the removal power in each case, and, for Union Ministers, it also sets out what follows if the Prime Minister gives no advice. Some details of the removal process are linked to the length of custody and to the seriousness of the offence. The Bill has drawn criticism from those who fear that it could be misused against opposition-led governments. Supporters argue that it keeps leaders from retaining power while facing serious charges, which is a question of constitutional morality. Together, these rules make the Bill a detailed scheme for ministers facing criminal proceedings.

quizzes.title: RPA and Court Rulings Check
quizzes.passage: Section 8 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, sets out when a legislator is disqualified because of a criminal conviction. The provision does not treat all offences alike. For some offences, a conviction alone is enough for disqualification, while for others the sentence imposed decides the matter. The Act also protects sitting members who challenge a conviction. Such a member can continue in the House for a limited period if an appeal is filed quickly, until the appeal is decided or the term ends, whichever is earlier. The Supreme Court has examined this area several times. In one ruling, it held that no constitutional bar prevents the appointment of a minister with a criminal background. In another, it held that only Parliament can legislate new grounds of disqualification, and that courts cannot add them. A later case from 2025 involved a minister who was reappointed after getting bail and who was asked to choose between freedom and office. He stepped down while his bail continued. The Bill under discussion differs from these rules because it links removal to arrest and detention rather than to a conviction. This difference explains why the Bill is read alongside the existing disqualification scheme in the Act.

quizzes.title: Ladakh and the AHDC expansion
quizzes.passage: Ladakh became a Union Territory without a Legislative Assembly in 2019, so decentralised local institutions have become central to governance. The Ladakh Administration has now approved the setting up of Autonomous Hill Development Councils across the region. Councils in each district will be set up through an official notification issued by the Government. This decision followed an in-principle agreement with the Ministry of Home Affairs, which aims to extend constitutional safeguards under Article 371 to the Union Territory. Until now, elected councils had existed in only a few parts of Ladakh, and the expansion will extend them to all districts. The people of Ladakh have raised several demands, including inclusion under the Sixth Schedule for constitutional protection, restrictions on land ownership to prevent an outside influx, and a Legislative Assembly for representative governance. Article 371 and the articles up to 371J give special constitutional safeguards to certain States and regions, with the aim of protecting indigenous culture, customary laws and local employment. Separately, the Centre has changed the rules for jobs and educational admissions in Ladakh through a new reservation regulation, which came into force shortly after it was approved. The regulation also modifies the reservation law of Jammu and Kashmir as applied to the region. The councils function under a separate Act and their powers are mainly administrative and developmental.

quizzes.title: Powers and finances of AHDCs
quizzes.passage: The Autonomous Hill Development Councils are created through legislation and apply only in Ladakh. Their powers are mainly administrative and developmental. The Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council Act gives the government the power to create councils in every district. The Act is therefore the legal basis for the councils and their functions. Every district of Ladakh is to have one such council, and each council works within the powers described above. The councils can exercise authority over land allotment, and they also have authority over district cadre recruitment and promotions. They prepare district development plans for sectors such as health, education, tourism, infrastructure and social welfare. Each council also has financial powers, and it can levy taxes, fees and other lawful charges. The councils do not have judicial authority. This is an important difference from the Sixth Schedule Autonomous District Councils, which can establish village courts under customary tribal laws. The Sixth Schedule councils also have legislative, executive, financial and judicial powers. The Sixth Schedule councils apply to tribal areas in certain northeastern States, while the AHDCs apply only in Ladakh. Ladakh has been administered as a Union Territory since 2019, and it has no Legislative Assembly. Decentralised local institutions are therefore central to how the region is governed.

quizzes.title: Delhi EV Policy 2.0 Overview Quiz

The policy will remain effective until 31 March 2030. It builds upon the achievements of the Delhi EV Policy 2020 and provides a comprehensive roadmap for transforming Delhi into a leading electric mobility hub. A central aim is to reduce vehicular emissions by encouraging the electrification of high-usage and high-emission transport segments. The policy sets an electrification target of at least 30 per cent of Delhi's total vehicle fleet by 31 March 2030. Several segments have been identified as priorities, including two-wheelers, three-wheelers, commercial goods carriers, school buses, app-based aggregator fleets and government-owned transport fleets. The policy also seeks to promote the widespread adoption of zero-emission vehicles, reduce urban air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions, and encourage sustainable public and commercial transport. It is linked to India's clean energy and climate commitments. The idea of electric mobility is not new in India. The National Electric Mobility Mission Plan, launched in 2013, set out an earlier national plan to expand the number of electric vehicles on the roads. Delhi's policy therefore sits within a longer national effort to shift transport away from petrol and diesel vehicles.

quizzes.title: ISA quick check
quizzes.passage: The International Solar Alliance is an international body set up to promote solar energy across the world. It is aimed at solar-rich countries that lie between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn, and it is described as a treaty-based intergovernmental organisation. The alliance states its aim as ensuring clean, reliable and affordable access to solar energy, which it links to sustainable growth and an improved quality of life. Its vision is a short phrase that asks members to work together to make the sun brighter. Membership rules have also widened over time. Countries from outside the tropics are allowed to join, although they are excluded from voting rights. Recognition from the wider United Nations system has also followed over the years. This makes the alliance a platform for solar-rich nations to coordinate their efforts. The alliance's mission goes beyond membership. It aims to provide clean energy access to a very large population and to mitigate solar-related emissions across the globe. It also seeks to promote low-cost, sustainable and equitable solar systems in the least developed countries and small island developing states. Together, these features give the alliance a clear geographic base, an inclusive membership and a practical focus on people who need energy access.

The government argues that this household-based system creates inequities within the AAY category, because small households end up receiving more foodgrain per person than larger households. Under the proposal, the entitlement would be worked out for each individual in the household, with an overall ceiling for each household. The government expects this to make distribution more proportional to household size and to align allocation more closely with nutritional requirements. The change would also reduce disparities between AAY households and Priority Households. The amendment, however, does not deal with inclusion errors. The National Food Security Act was enacted to ensure food and nutritional security through subsidised foodgrains delivered by a targeted system. The households concerned belong to the poorest group within the Act. The proposal is still under consideration and is discussed here as a change in the making, so its final shape may differ from what is described above.

quizzes.title: Tariffs, market access and trade deal terms
quizzes.passage:
The India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement, known as CETA, is described as a next-generation free trade agreement. It goes beyond conventional tariff reduction and addresses market access, regulatory transparency and economic partnership. The scope of the deal is wide, covering trade in goods and services along with digital trade and investment. The framework also reaches government procurement, labour, environment, innovation, small and medium enterprises and regulatory cooperation. In this sense the agreement is broader than a simple list of duty cuts, since these areas show it addresses far more than goods moving across borders.

Tariff policy in the deal aims to balance two goals. Domestic industry is protected, while foreign goods gain access to the market in phases rather than all at once. Passenger vehicles show this balance clearly, since imports of these vehicles are handled through a quota arrangement.

The deal is also tied to predictability in trade. Countries are looking for stable and predictable trade relations amid geopolitical tensions and tariff disputes. A bilateral agreement offers a framework that reduces this uncertainty and supports long-term growth for both partners.

Taken together, these features show that the agreement combines tariff reduction with wider economic cooperation between the two countries.

quizzes.title: Brexit and the UK's exit from the EU
quizzes.passage:
The European Union is an economic and political union, and it allows free trade among member countries without checks or extra charges. Membership was not permanent, however. A national vote in the UK led to a decision to leave, and the process that followed involved long political debate.

Once the decision was made, the UK had to plan a different future. Leaving the bloc meant losing the market access that membership gave, so London began looking for new trade partnerships to support growth. The arrangement that governed the exit also allowed a phase in which Britain continued to follow EU laws and rules for a set period. The change marked a major shift in Britain's trade position.

Other countries were changing their trade choices too. Many western nations wanted to reduce their dependence on China, and several saw India as a China-plus-one alternative. At the same time, geopolitical tensions and tariff disputes encouraged governments to seek stable and predictable trade relations. This reflected a wider shift in how governments viewed their trade relationships.

India also reshaped its approach. Rather than remaining in larger regional groupings, it moved its focus toward bilateral agreements that protect its interests. Such agreements are seen as a way to reduce uncertainty for business and long-term trade.

quizzes.title: Polymer Notes: Concept and History
quizzes.passage: Currency notes in India are usually printed on cotton-based banknote paper, but the Reserve Bank of India is now looking at a different material. The RBI has revived a proposal to introduce durable polymer-based banknotes, which are made from a specialised plastic material instead of paper. The Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited, a printing subsidiary wholly owned by the RBI, has invited global bids for a polymer substrate suitable for making such notes. Australia has already gone further, having introduced a complete series of polymer banknotes. Supporters of the idea point to the durability of plastic notes, which can withstand frequent use in circulation. The challenges, however, include cost, the need for new machines and the handling of plastic waste. The proposal therefore combines an old policy idea with a fresh push from the central bank. Polymer notes are therefore a topic of both economic and policy interest, since they involve printing, cost and environmental questions. The discussion covers the material, the printing arrangements and the financial trade-offs involved. quizzes.title: Currency Management Basics
quizzes.passage: Currency management in India is shared between the government and the Reserve Bank of India. Currency and coinage fall within the legislative domain of the Union government, and the central bank handles much of the day-to-day work. The RBI issues banknotes, estimates how much currency the country requires and tries to maintain an adequate supply of notes. It also ensures that the notes in circulation are of good quality. Banknote designs and materials are approved by the government, based on recommendations from the RBI Central Board. Coins follow a different path. The government designs and mints them, and once minted they are supplied to the RBI. The RBI then distributes coins to banks and the public through its currency management network. Banknotes themselves are printed at facilities run by two different kinds of organisation, one a government enterprise and the other a company owned by the RBI. Together they print notes in many denominations for the whole country. Each body has a clearly defined role in the system. Banknote printing and coin production are handled through different channels, so the roles are easy to confuse. This division of work is a useful theme for economics and current affairs, because it shows how government and central bank responsibilities are separated.

quizzes.title: SDG evolution check
quizzes.passage: Sustainable development began as a defined concept before it became a set of global targets. A commission first defined the idea, and global meetings then built on that definition over the following decades. Early efforts focused on a small group of development goals. Later conferences followed up on these efforts, and they pushed the world to think beyond the original list. The eventual result was a broader framework covering poverty, health, education, gender equality, climate and peace. This framework was built as one agenda, with goals that were meant to be integrated with one another. Each annual review uses a score on a common scale, so that countries can be compared and their results can be read by policymakers and the public. Reviews of this kind are published every year, and they show how far each nation has moved toward the goals. Some regions have improved faster than others, while some targets have moved backwards, which shows that progress has been uneven. Looking back, the path from a concept to a framework took several decades and many meetings. Such a wide agenda made it possible to track progress across many different areas, even though it also made measurement more demanding.

quizzes.title: Earth Summit recall
quizzes.passage: The United Nations Conference on Environment and Development was a major meeting held in Brazil, and it is widely remembered as the Earth Summit. Its central aim was to make the world see that environmental protection and sustainable development had to be pursued together. The conference adopted several documents. The first was a short statement of guiding principles, which stressed the precautionary approach, the polluter pays principle and common but differentiated responsibilities. The second was an action plan that was not legally binding, but it addressed poverty, sustainable consumption and the protection of fragile environments. This plan gave a stronger role to major groups such as women and indigenous people, and it offered a framework for action at local, national and global levels. The third document dealt with forests, and its principles were also not legally binding. These principles covered the conservation of forests and the sustainable management of all types of forests. Taken together, the outcomes of the conference laid part of the groundwork for later international agreements, including several that followed in the years after the summit. Many of these ideas were later revisited at summits held over the following decades, which kept the discussion active. Its outcomes were framed as guidance and action plans rather than as binding treaties.

quizzes.title: Vikram-1 Mission Check
quizzes.passage: Skyroot Aerospace, a company based in Hyderabad, has launched Vikram-1, India's first privately built orbital launch vehicle. The rocket flew its maiden mission, called Mission Aagaman, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota. The flight placed payloads into Low Earth Orbit and made India the third country to demonstrate private orbital launch capability. Vikram-1 carries a combination of scientific, technological, commercial and symbolic payloads. Vikram-1 was developed by Skyroot Aerospace, a company whose developers include Pawan Kumar Chandana and Naga Bharath Daka. Rockets of two broad kinds help explain the achievement. A sub-orbital rocket travels into space but does not place a satellite into orbit. An orbital rocket places a satellite into orbit around the Earth. quizzes.passage:
Ladakh became a Union Territory without a Legislative Assembly in 2019, and this made decentralised local institutions central to its governance. The Ladakh Administration has approved the establishment of Autonomous Hill Development Councils in all seven districts. The step follows an in-principle agreement with the Ministry of Home Affairs to extend constitutional safeguards under Article 371 to the Union Territory.

The Autonomous Hill Development Councils can be compared with the Autonomous District Councils that the Sixth Schedule provides for. The comparison looks at how each body is created, where it applies and what powers it holds, and the two bodies differ on each of these points. Article 371 and Articles 371A to 371J are placed in Part XXI of the Constitution, and together they provide special constitutional safeguards to certain States and regions.

quizzes.title: PDS History and PMGKAY

Its coverage has changed as different groups of people were brought within its scope, and its design has been adjusted in response to conditions in different parts of the country. Governance involves both the central and state governments, and a central ministry is responsible for overseeing the system at the national level. Some states built their own distribution arrangements well before the wider expansion, while others followed later. quizzes.title: Climate Finance: Sources and Funds
quizzes.passage:
Climate finance refers to money that supports action against climate change, and it can come from local, national or transnational sources. Such action has two broad aims: reducing emissions, and helping communities adapt to the effects of climate change. Several multilateral funds have been set up to channel resources to these aims, and each fund has its own role and procedures. Their approaches differ, and some are designed around the needs of particular groups of countries. The arrangements include a number of different funds, each with its own structure, which is why the subject can seem complex.

Climate finance also rests on a set of principles that guide how responsibility is shared among countries.
